catalog_quote: A Chinantec word consists of one or more syllables, only one of which is stressed—usually the last. The major lexical classes are usually realized as a single stressed syllable, but there are also a substantial number of complex verb and noun stems having a pretonic syllable as well. A handful of verbal prefixes and a few proclitic functors provide further sources for pretonic syllables. [...] Grammatical inflection for person-of-subject (in verbs) or possessor (in nouns) is the source of a posttonic unstressed syllable in that pronouns occur in both a FULL form as stressed syllables and in a REDUCED unstressed form with limited segmental and tonal properties. [...] There are two kinds of word stress, ballistic and controlled. A ballistic syllable (= syllable with ballistic stress) is characterized by a surge and rapid decay of intensity with a resultant fortis articulation of its consonantal onset and a tendency to loss of voicing resulting in a breathy release toward the end. A controlled syllable displays a more constant level of intensity throughout its duration and is typically longer that a ballistic syllable. [...] A ballistic syllable is marked by an acute accent /´/ over its nuclear vowel. A controlled syllable is unmarked (for the sake of simplifying the notation), but is distinguished from unstressed syllables in a controlled word of more than one syllable as the last syllable marked for contrastive tone.
world_status: statement found in an open source

I rendered p.14 (printed p.4, opening of Anderson, Martinez & Pace 'Comaltepec Chinantec tone') to an image and read it directly: the quoted passage is there word for word -- 'A Chinantec word consists of one or more syllables, only one of which is stressed—usually the last. The major lexical classes are usually realized as a single stressed syllable, but there are also a substantial number of complex verb and noun stems having a pretonic syllable as well. A handful of verbal prefixes and a few proclitic functors provide further so…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Each word has exactly one stressed syllable, the root/stem syllable, which is normally word-final; pretonic syllables (first syllables of complex stems, verbal prefixes, proclitics) are unstressed and carry a reduced set of three level tones; the only posttonic syllables are reduced enclitic subject/possessor pronouns, whose tone is predictable. The stressed syllable is additionally either ballistic or controlled (a lexical/inflectional syllable-type contrast, not a positional one).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; unstressed pretonic syllables keep (reduced) tonal contrasts, posttonic syllables have predictable tone.
new_statements.exceptions: 'usually the last': the exception is words with a reduced (enclitic) person-of-subject or possessor pronoun, which adds a posttonic unstressed syllable after the stressed root (e.g. lá'LM-a 'I buy it'); syllable-final /r b/ enclitics attach to the stressed syllable itself. Ballistic vs controlled is a contrast among stressed syllables, both lexical and used in verb inflection.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word including proclitics and enclitic pronouns; most lexical words are monosyllabic, so the rule is visible mainly in complex stems (hmiL-sí̃HL 'cat'), prefixed verbs (kaL-hmiL-hmí:H 'I melted it') and encliticized forms. Language is fully tonal (L, M, H, LM, LH, HM, HL on the stressed syllable).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the Chinantec of Santiago Comaltepec, Ixtlán de Juárez, Oaxaca (ISO cco = Glottolog coma1246); principal consultant for the 1990 tone paper was Isaac H. Martínez of Comaltepec. Silverman's ELL2 entry is pan-Chinantecan but its pre-/post-tonic sentences are explicitly about Comaltepec. Note for the catalog: in Chinantecanist usage 'ballistic vs controlled stress' is a syllable-type (phonation/intensity) contrast on the single stressed syllable, not a difference in stress position.

new_statements.quote: 1.4. Stress. There are two kinds of syllable stress, ballistic and controlled (Merrifield 1963). Ballistic stress is a combination of pitch and stress. It tends to raise high tones and lower low tones. The ballistic syllable is marked by an acute accent /´/ over its nuclear vowel. A controlled syllable is unmarked. lo:L 'skin', ló:LH 'lime'. [p. 3] — Three consonants /b n r/ may occur syllable-finally. Of these, /b r/ always constitute a separate morpheme in this position; only /-n/ occurs as a final consonant in morphemically simple forms, as in bé:nL 'bud, shoot'. For this reason, syllable-final /b r/ are written in this study as posttonic material, following the stressed syllable. [p. 2]
new_statements.citation: Anderson, Judi L. (1989). Comaltepec Chinantec Syntax. Dallas, Texas: The Summer Institute of Linguistics and the University of Texas at Arlington. xiv+119 pp.

It tends to raise high tones and lower low tones. The ballistic syllable is marked by an acute accent /'/ over its nuclear vowel. A controlled syllable is unmarked. lo:L 'skin', ló:LH 'lime'.' The p. 2 passage ('Three consonants /b n r/ may occur syllable-finally.. syllable-final /b r/ are written in this study as posttonic material, following the stressed syllable') is verbat…
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing Anderson/Martínez/Pace 1990 statement (one stressed syllable = the stem; pretonic prefixes, posttonic enclitics). Adds that 'stress' in Comaltepec is a two-way ballistic/controlled contrast on the stressed syllable (p. 3) and that enclitic pronouns and /b r/ are posttonic unstressed material; it does not itself state 'usually the last' or any positional rule, so it refines rather than independently confirms placement. The listed open URLs (sil.org/acpub/repository/ and) now return 404; the SIL archive record pagehttps://www.sil.org/resources/archives/8881(HTTP 200) lists at 1,479,157 bytes, identical in size to the on-disk file, which was downloaded earlier from…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The book gives no placement rule. It presupposes one stressed syllable per word (the lexical stem/root), describes the ballistic-vs-controlled contrast on that stressed syllable, calls tense/aspect prefixes 'pretonic' (§2.11) and reduced person enclitics 'posttonic' unstressed material (p. 2; p. 72 fn. 1: an enclitic -na:? 'would be the only known unstressed syllable in the language having a long vowel'). So stress sits on the stem, with unstressed prefixal and enclitic syllables around it; the ballistic/controlled type is a lexical/inflectional property of the stressed syllable, not a placement rule.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 72 fn. 1: the second-plural pronoun ná?L is treated as 'a normal, stressed syllable' (a fully-stressed phonological word) although it patterns syntactically with the enclitic (unstressed) pronoun forms; ballistic vs controlled stress is contrastive on the stressed syllable (lo:L 'skin' vs ló:LH 'lime') and takes part in verb inflection (§2.2, p. 5: 'A combination of tone, ballistic stress, and segmental changes define these categories').
new_statements.identity_note: Both Comaltepec chapters and the 1989 grammar describe the variety of Santiago Comaltepec, Ixtlán de Juárez, Oaxaca (AMP p. 3 fn. 1: about 1000 residents; data from 1970 on, principal language associate Isaac Martínez). The Merrifield & Rensch volume also contains chapters on Lealao Chinantec (Rupp; Rensch) and Quiotepec Chinantec (Gardner & Merrifield) and a comparative chapter on motion verbs ('Moving and arriving in the Chinantla'); those are other Chinantec languages and were not used for coma1246.

new_statements.relation_note: This volume is the source of the catalog's existing statement (AMP 1990 p. 4, reading 'morphologically determined'); the quoted sentence is verbatim on printed p. 4 (p. 14). Pace's chapter (p. 22) adds the explicit statement that the verb root is always the stressed syllable and that pretonic/posttonic syllables are unstressed, which sharpens 'usually the last' into stem-stress. The other chapters (Rupp, 'The Lealao Chinantec syllable', p. 63: 'The stressed syllable is the last syllable of the word unless the word ends with one of five unstressed person markers'; Gardner & Merrifield, 'Quiotepec Chinantec tone', p. 92: 'A word consists of one or more syllables, only one of which is stressed…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stressed syllable per word, which is the syllable of the lexical stem (verb root or noun stem); it is 'usually the last' syllable because prefixes, proclitics and the first syllable of complex stems are pretonic (unstressed, only three level tones L M H allowed, AMP §3.1 p. 15), while reduced person-of-subject/possessor pronouns are posttonic unstressed syllables that can follow it. The stressed syllable is further either ballistic or controlled ('two kinds of word stress', p. 4); in a controlled polysyllabic word the stressed syllable is identified as 'the last syllable marked for contrastive tone' (p. 4).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned; pretonic and posttonic syllables are simply 'unstressed'.
new_statements.exceptions: AMP p. 20 fn.: a small group of interrogative words (hieHM 'where?', etc.) is exceptional for the /HM/ glide (tone, not stress). Pace p. 22: 'the verb root never occurs unstressed'; unstressed pretonic/posttonic syllables are 'not, in general, affected by inflection'. Pace p. 51: the pretonic first syllable of disyllabic verbs keeps its citation tone (low) throughout the paradigm, or, if high, is high in first-person forms and low elsewhere.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Comaltepec chapters and the 1989 grammar describe the variety of Santiago Comaltepec, Ixtlán de Juárez, Oaxaca (AMP p. 3 fn. 1: about 1000 residents; data from 1970 on, principal language associate Isaac Martínez). tone_statements.quote: The tones listed in 3a are attested in morphologically simplex environments. Those in 3b may be found in phonologically or morphologically derived environments. An example of each tone is presented. ... (3) a. Simplex tones L hi˩ 'book' H ... 'pretty' M ku:˧ 'money' LM ... 'swing' LH ... 'tepejilote palm shoot' b. Derived tones HL ... '(give) a banana' HM ... '(give) money' MH ... 'is it (his)' ... First, the Comaltepec tonal inventory is comparatively rich, with five lexical tonal patterns, and several allophonic and morphologically complex variants.
tone_statements.locator: p.476, sec.2, ex. (3); last sentence p.479, sec.3
tone_statements.summary: Five lexical tones L, H, M, LM, LH plus derived HL, HM, MH; sandhi = rightward H spread from LH syllables; words mostly monosyllabic. Data credited to Anderson et al. 1990.

tone_statements.quote: A stressed syllable may occur (1) with any of three simple tones: low /ᴸ/, mid /ᴹ/, or high /ᴴ/; or (2) with any of four tone sequences: two upglides (low-mid /ᴸᴹ/ or low-high /ᴸᴴ/) and two downglides (high-mid /ᴴᴹ/ or high-low /ᴴᴸ/). ... Taking into consideration the eight kinds of syllables and seven tone configurations (three levels and four glides), there are fifty-six potential combinations of tone and syllable type.
tone_statements.locator: p.8 sec.1.7 Tone; second sentence p.16 sec.4 Discussion
tone_statements.summary: 3 level tones + 4 glides on the stressed syllable (tone letters are raised capitals); HL, HM said to be derived by sandhi, L M H LM LH basic. Ballistic vs controlled stress cross-classifies with tone.

sources.quote: The tones listed in 3a are attested in morphologically simplex environments. Those in 3b may be found in phonologically or morphologically derived environments. [...] All data in this section are culled from the thoroughgoing descriptions in Anderson 1989, Anderson et al. 1990, and Pace 1990. (3) a. Simplex tones: L 'book', H 'pretty', M 'money', LM 'swing', LH 'tepejilote palm shoot'; b. Derived tones: HL '(give) a banana', HM '(give) money', MH 'is it (his)'. [...] As stated in the introduction, Comaltepec tone sandhi normally involves the rightward spreading of H tones from LH syllables. [...] Moreover, Comaltepec words are normally monosyllabic, while verbal inflection usually involves tone modification. [...] Yet Comaltepec tone sandhi is indeed rampant, regularly taking place both word-internally (upon encliticization, and in rare polysyllabic roots) and across word boundaries (Anderson et al. 1990:13). It is impeded only by a pause, or by a topic-comment boundary (Pace 1990:26).
